title: Opus X's debt to Lunceford Special and Parker's added solo
summary: He later realizes the alto interlude copies a Lunceford arrangement, and Parker asks to add a solo that transforms the piece.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: And I had another place in there where there was a little written interlude for the alto saxophone player. It was kind of in the style of some things that I had heard Willie Smith do with the Jimmy Lunceford band. As a matter of fact, I learned later that the piece that I wrote was actually a steal from one of Jimmy Lunceford's arrangements that I had not realized. A lot of times, a young musician will write something that he's heard, and actually it will be very similar or almost a carbon copy of something, maybe with a little variation of something that he's heard, and he doesn't even realize it.. I learned years later that this happened to be a thing that Jimmy Lunceford had, called "Lunceford Special." And my "Opus X" was almost...very similar to that. But what I did, I took that theme and I took it in a different
direction, using some of the things that I had heard Sy Oliver and Eddie Durham use with the Lunceford band.

Anyway, this alto thing was for about 8 bars. And there was no solo in the piece at all. Charlie Parker asked me, he said, "John, would you mind if I put a solo in there?" I said, "No, man, that would be great!" So after that little interlude thing and everything, Charlie Parker took off and played a solo. He'd play anywhere from three to five choruses or whatever, as long as he wanted to play. It turned the whole tune around. It made a different tune out of it altogether.

So Billy, when we got ready to do this recording date, he said he was going to use this tune. And I was just overjoyed, because except for a little thing that I had written with Trummy Young which I never did anything, I had never had anything on record before.
